bearings.paper_claim: Influence accrues per legislator pair as a decayed ratio C_pass / C_tot of mutually cosponsored bills that eventually pass the House. Sponsor and cosponsor are treated identically, edges are undirected, decay is monthly with half-life 6, 12 or 24 months, and scores are normalized by party size (Eq. 1-4). Passage means House passage. The authors call the result only a proxy (p. 17).
bearings.system_side: Brain cites this paper for the CU cosponsor edge weights. Code (congress_member_scraper.R lines 1776-1788 and 1923-1936; fec/network/build_holistic_base.py) builds weight = role (original 1.0, regular 0.5; holistic regular 0.2) x 3.0 if the last action matches the passage regex x 0.8 per Congress of age x 1/sqrt(C), summed per directed sponsor-to-cosponsor pair. This is a volume-weighted success boost, not a pass/total ratio, with no party normalization. Last-action caveat (build_holistic_base.py, 2026-08-17): 2,652 of 37,076 tie-contributing bills carry 39,390 of 410,411 ties (about 9.6 percent); scoring them as passed would raise unrolled tie weight about 14.9 percent.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper supports only the general idea of weighting ties by joint passage, for House bills 2009-2019 with House passage as outcome. It gives no evidence for the x3 multiplier, the 1/sqrt(C) discount, the 2:1 or 5:1 role ratio, the per-Congress decay, Senate ties or CU-topic bill universes. Read the citation as inspired by, not implements.
bearings.verifier_note: Paper claims and numbers checked against text pp. 5-9 and p. 17. R and holistic constants confirmed in code. Summary 14.9 percent figure misread the caveat (it is the rise in tie weight, not the affected share), corrected here. Summary additive wording for the x3 factor corrected here.

bearings.paper_claim: Eigenvector centrality on the decayed pass/total matrix (largest connected component) barely separates passed from failed bills: relative difference 0.004 (mean) and 0.002 (max), against 0.139 and 0.248 for the influence score. Closeness (0.004 / 0.002) and strength (0.004 / 0.003) are equally weak. The authors suspect network density but do not test it.
bearings.system_side: InfluenceScore = 0.60 weighted out-degree + 0.25 betweenness + 0.15 eigenvector, min-max normalized and rescaled to 0-100, on the success-weighted directed cosponsor graph. Weights confirmed in code. The retirement from Influence percent (AB13 = 0) and the underdog-lens use were not found in a search of fec/ or the Draft Systems R script, so they remain unverified.
bearings.transfer_conditions: This backs the retirement only loosely. The paper's centralities use a different matrix (ratio, undirected, House 2009-2019) and it never tests betweenness or weighted out-degree. Answering the component's open question on the system graph would be circular: weighted out-degree sums ties on the member's own sponsored bills, which are already multiplied by 3 when the bill passed. A passage test needs an as-of network built only from bills resolved before the outcome window.
bearings.verifier_note: Paper numbers match text pp. 14-21; density suspicion confirmed at p. 19. InfluenceScore weights confirmed in code. AB13 retirement and underdog use not located, so not confirmed.

bearings.paper_claim: The paper measures whether bill-level aggregates of cosponsors' pairwise pass-rate scores separate passed from failed bills. It does not study recruitment, paths, ask success or per-edge probabilities. It never compares its measure against raw cosponsor count; it only cites prior work that cosponsor count is not a clear signal of success (pp. 3-4, refs 29 and 23).
bearings.system_side: Template comment (make_dashboard_html_00.tpl lines 735-738) cites the paper for 'cosponsorship influence, not count, drives passage' as grounding for a PROVABLY-OPTIMAL max-product recruitment chain. It calls the chain reliability the exact maximal probability that the chain holds ('mathematical certainty'). Code computes chainHold as a product of activeP values with ASKM = 0.07 (lines 728-760).
bearings.transfer_conditions: None. The paper's outcome is bill passage, not whether a target joins as cosponsor, and its score is not a probability. The citation overstates what the paper shows, and the probability wording conflicts with D-025.
bearings.verifier_note: Template wording and citation confirmed at lines 735-738; the quoted phrase is exact. The paper's count discussion spans pp. 3-4, not p. 4 alone.

bearings.paper_claim: A decayed pass/total success ratio is informative about outcomes. Passed bills carry higher cosponsor pass-ratio influence than failed bills in every 4-month window (relative difference 0.139 mean / 0.248 max at a 6-month half-life). The authors contrast their approach with LES, which has no decay and splits the process into finer stages.
bearings.system_side: Efficiency term per (member, category) = sum(decay x sign x advanced) / sum(decay) over sponsored and original-cosponsored bills, excluding unknown outcomes. Blended with the agenda term via percentranks. Confirmed in code.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Indirect support only. The paper's ratio is pairwise, aggregated to bills, and includes each bill's own outcome. The pillar's ratio is member-level and describes CU-topic advancement; the paper does not show that a member's success rate measures CU influence or predicts future behaviour. The paper pools across parties and 2009-2019 with no strata, so label UNSTRATIFIED. The authors report a decline from about 2015 and hypothesize it is correlated with polarization.
bearings.verifier_note: Numbers and code confirmed. The summary wording that the authors themselves say influence fell is an overstatement; the paper hypothesizes correlation with polarization (p. 13).

bearings.paper_claim: Shorter decay gives slightly more separation within the tested range: relative differences 0.248, 0.223 and 0.203 at 6, 12 and 24-month half-lives (SE 0.0139, 0.0119, 0.0107). The paper lists a comparison with LES as future work and does not run it.
bearings.system_side: Shadow uses Volden-Wiseman-style stages with role weights 3/2/1, a 180-day cosponsor timing half-life and congress decay 0.8 (confirmed in code). The 0.8 per Congress equals a half-life of about 3.1 Congresses, far longer than the 24-month maximum the paper tested.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper proposes an LES comparison; it does not propose a sub-Congress decay check, and it already tested 6 and 12-month half-lives. Its outcome (separating passed from failed bills) differs from the shadow's goal (convergence with LES), so it cannot set the decay value. Its evidence covers only 6-24 months.
bearings.verifier_note: Figures and SEs confirmed. Code constants confirmed. The suggests framing in the analyst transfer text goes beyond the paper and is corrected here.

bearings.paper_claim: The 6-month half-life is one of three settings for decaying cosponsorship-influence capital, not a stance-salience estimate. Discrimination barely changes between 6 and 24 months (0.248 vs 0.203).
bearings.system_side: Media blend decays each post by 0.5^(age/HL): HL 2.0 years for press and SOCIAL_HL_YEARS default 0.5 for social (confirmed in build_media_blend.py).
bearings.transfer_conditions: Not transferable. The paper's decay applies to accrued passage-rate ties and its outcome is bill passage. Its flatness across half-lives warns against treating any one value as calibrated. The paper does not justify 0.5 years for social posts or 2 years for press.
bearings.verifier_note: Paper values and code half-lives confirmed.

related.why: Paper cites Porter, Mucha, Newman and Warmbrand 2005 (ref 19) and lists committee assignments as a missing control (p. 17). Porter is the second author here, not the senior author.
Not cited in this paper. The dashboard template comment (make_dashboard_html_00.tpl line 738) cites Chen et al. 2016 next to this paper, so the co-citation exists only in the repo.

summary_issues: Summary says there are no significance tests. The paper reports standard errors (error bars; SE 0.0139, 0.0119, 0.0107) but no formal tests, controls or strata. Reword.

Summary calls the x3 success factor an additive multiplier. In code it multiplies each passed-bill tie by 3 before summing, so it is a volume weight. A garbled character stands in for the multiplication sign.

system_side and summary misread the holistic caveat: 14.9 percent is the rise in unrolled tie weight if the 2,652 affected bills were scored as passed, not the share of tie weight affected (about 9.6 percent, 39,390 of 410,411 ties).
flags: the paper does not attribute the post-2015 decline to polarization. It hypothesizes the decline is correlated with polarization (p. 13).
